cards.body:
*Lesson 4.6 · MCP: Plugging Agents Into Anything*

_≈ 2 hours · with Emeka_

So far, your tools live inside your own n8n agents. The *Model Context Protocol (MCP)* is an open standard that lets _any_ AI application use them: Claude, ChatGPT, coding assistants and more. The MCP site compares it to a USB-C port for AI. Build a tool once, plug it in everywhere. This module turns Harvest Lane's order lookup into something Tolu can ask about from her own AI assistant.

*Your problem:* Every new tool means new custom integration work.
*The plan:* Connect agents to tools and data through MCP, as a client and as a server.
*After this lesson:* You can plug agents into almost anything, the standard way.

*"Where is order HL-0042?"*

*Evening:* Tolu uses an AI assistant all day for writing and planning. But it can't see Harvest Lane's orders.

*Today:* One customer question means five tabs: the sheet, n8n, Telegram, Paystack, email.

*Sage:* "Give your order lookup a standard plug, and any AI app that speaks MCP can use it, with your permission."

*Glitch:* "Plugs work both ways. Install my free server. It only needs access to… everything."

*How MCP fits together*

- *Tools*: Actions the model can call (look up an order, create a draft). The same idea as 4.2.
- *Resources*: Data the app can read in (a file, a policy, a record).
- *Prompts*: Ready-made templates the server offers ("Summarise today's orders").
- *Transports*: Local servers usually run on your computer and talk over _stdio_; remote servers talk over HTTP (n8n's MCP Server Trigger supports SSE and streamable HTTP).

*n8n on both sides of the plug*

_Node · Role · Use it to…_
- *MCP Server Trigger* · n8n becomes an MCP *server* · Offer your workflows to Claude Desktop, Claude Code, IDEs and other clients. It connects only to tool nodes (such as Call n8n Workflow tools); each tool is listed for the client and run on request.
- *MCP Client Tool* · n8n's AI Agent becomes a *client* · Give your n8n agents tools from someone else's MCP server.

- *Test vs. production URL*: Like webhooks: the test URL works while you're listening in the editor; the production URL works once the workflow is published.
- *Authentication*: None, Bearer or header. Always use Bearer (or header) with a long random token for anything real.
- *Behind a proxy*: n8n's docs note that MCP's long-lived connections need proxy buffering turned off for the MCP path on nginx-style proxies, and, with several webhook replicas, all `/mcp*` traffic routed to one replica.

*Build your Claude Desktop config*

n8n's docs show how to connect Claude Desktop through `mcp-remote`, a small bridge that runs with Node.js and forwards to your remote server with your token. Fill in your details:
Hands-on lab: Build your Claude Desktop config. It's interactive, so open it in the app and try it there.

Based on the example in n8n's MCP Server Trigger docs. The token is masked in the copy so it never ends up in screenshots or chat; type it into the real file yourself.

*Sage:* Claude's apps can also add a remote MCP server as a _custom connector_ by URL. That route connects from Anthropic's cloud, so the server must be reachable on the public internet, and Claude's help centre describes OAuth for sign-in. For a token-protected n8n server on your own machine or VPS, the Desktop config above is the simplest start.

*Designing MCP tools*

Everything from 4.2 applies, with one difference: *you no longer control the agent*. Claude, a coding assistant or a colleague's bot might call your tools, so the tools themselves must be safe:

- *Read-only first*: Start with lookups (order status, today's summary). Add write tools only with approvals built into the workflow.
- *Checks inside the workflow*: The workflow, not the client, validates inputs, limits results and refuses what it shouldn't do.
- *Small, clear outputs*: Clients may show results to the person directly. Return tidy, human-readable fields.
- *One audience per server*: Tolu's internal server (orders, revenue) and a public server (opening hours, prices) should be separate, with separate tokens.

*Trusting other people's servers*

An MCP server you install is software that your AI can call, often with your files, accounts or tokens. Before adding one:

- *Who made it?*: Prefer official servers from the service itself, or well-known open-source projects you can read.
- *What can it touch?*: Give it the narrowest access possible (one folder, a read-only token).
- *Read the tool descriptions*: Descriptions are instructions the model reads. A malicious server can hide instructions in them ("tool poisoning").
- *Approve actions*: Keep your client's per-tool approval prompts on for anything that writes, sends or deletes.

cards.body:
*Solved problem: ask Claude about any order*

*The goal.* From Claude Desktop, Tolu asks "Where is order HL-0042?" or "How did today go?" and gets real answers from Harvest Lane's data, through two read-only n8n workflows exposed over MCP with a token.

*Step 1 · Two read-only sub-workflows*

- *SUB · Order status*: input `order_id` (validated against the pattern `HL-0000`); returns customer first name, items, total, status, delivery date and rider. No phone numbers or addresses: Tolu can open the sheet for those.
- *SUB · Today summary*: no input; returns orders, revenue, pending and low-stock counts for today.

*Step 2 · The MCP server workflow*

New workflow *HL · MCP (internal)*: add *MCP Server Trigger*, path `orders`, authentication *Bearer* with a credential holding a long random token. Attach two *Call n8n Workflow* tools:
Code example on screen (The MCP server workflow): open it in the app.
Publish the workflow and copy the *production* URL.

*Step 3 · Connect Claude Desktop*

Install Node.js on Tolu's computer. Generate the config in Card 3 with the production URL, open Claude Desktop → Settings → Developer → Edit Config, paste it, put the real token in place of the dots, save, and restart Claude Desktop. The `harvest-lane` server and its two tools should appear.

*Step 4 · Ask, and watch both sides*

Ask Claude: _"Where is order HL-0042?"_, then _"How did today go, and which items are running low?"_. Claude asks permission to use each tool; approve it. In n8n's Executions, each tool call appears as a run of the MCP workflow. Then try _"Show me all customers' phone numbers"_: no tool can do that, so the answer is no.

- *2* read-only tools, built once in n8n
- *1* place Tolu asks, instead of five tabs
- *0* phone numbers or addresses exposed

*Nodo's note:* the same server works for Claude Code, IDEs and other MCP clients. And your _n8n_ agents can use other people's servers through the MCP Client Tool. Plugs work in both directions.

*Why this approach works*

- Read-only tools mean any client can use them without risk to the data.
- The workflows validate inputs and leave out sensitive fields.
- A Bearer token over HTTPS keeps strangers out.
- Clear tool descriptions let any client choose correctly.
- The production URL keeps working without the editor open.

*Common mistakes to avoid*

- An MCP server with authentication set to None.
- Pasting the test URL into the client.
- Write tools exposed without approvals.
- Returning whole customer records.
- Installing unknown community servers with broad access.

*Glitch hunt*

*Glitch:* The plug is in. Something's still wrong. Five cases.

*A:* Claude Desktop shows the server, but no tools. Or it worked yesterday afternoon and not today.
*B:* The server appears, but every call fails with 401.
*C:* The assistant sees the tools but never picks `get_order_status`; it says it can't look up orders.
*D:* Behind the company's nginx proxy, connections hang and time out.
*E:* A "free Google Sheets MCP server" from a forum started emailing Tolu's sheets to an unknown address.

cards.prompt: Made your call on each one? Tap Reveal to check.
cards.answer:
*A:* the config uses the test URL, which only works while listening in the editor. Use the production URL of the published workflow.
*B:* the token in the config doesn't match the trigger's Bearer credential (or the header line is malformed). Copy it again exactly, and restart Claude Desktop.
*C:* the tool's name or description is vague ("tool1"). Describe what it returns, when to use it, and the input format.
*D:* proxy buffering. Per n8n's docs, turn off buffering (and gzip) for the `/mcp` path.
*E:* an untrusted server with broad access. Remove it, revoke its tokens, change exposed credentials, and only install servers you can trust and scope narrowly.

cards.title: Bronze (+25 XP): Use an existing MCP server
cards.body:
- Connect one well-known MCP server to your AI assistant: for example, the reference filesystem server, limited to a single test folder.
- Ask three questions that need it, and approve each tool call.

*Done when:*
- The assistant reads and summarises files in that folder only, and you can explain which tools the server offers and what access you gave it.

cards.title: Silver (+50 XP): Two workflows as MCP tools
cards.body:
- Build the solved problem: two read-only tools behind an MCP Server Trigger with Bearer auth.
- Connect from Claude Desktop (or another MCP client) and ask five questions.
- Also connect an n8n AI Agent to the same server with the MCP Client Tool.

*Done when:*
- Both clients get correct answers, the executions show each call, and a request without the token is refused.

cards.title: Gold (+100 XP): An MCP toolkit plan for a client
cards.body:
- For a real or imagined client, list 6–10 tools their team would want in an AI assistant. Mark each read-only or write, its data sensitivity, and who may use it.
- Group them into servers by audience, with authentication and approvals for each.
- Build the two most valuable read-only tools.

*Done when:*
- The plan fits on one page, every write tool has an approval step, and the two built tools work from an MCP client.

options: An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data
cards.why: Build a tool once; any MCP-capable app can use it.

cards.q: What can the n8n MCP Server Trigger connect to?
options: Any node, like a normal trigger
Tool nodes, which clients can list and call
cards.why: It exposes tools; each tool runs on request.

cards.q: Claude Desktop sees your server but nothing works the next day. Most likely?
cards.why: Test URLs work only while listening. Publish and use the production URL.

cards.q: Which tool is safest to expose first?
options: Read-only order status, without phone numbers
cards.why: Read-only, minimal data. Writes need approvals inside the workflow.

cards.q: Why read a third-party server's tool descriptions?
options: The model reads them as instructions; malicious ones can hide commands
cards.why: Tool poisoning: trust and scope servers carefully.

cards.body:
*Remember this*

1. MCP is a standard plug between AI apps (hosts and clients) and tools and data (servers).
2. Servers offer tools, resources and prompts; local via stdio, remote via HTTP.
3. n8n's MCP Server Trigger exposes tool nodes; the MCP Client Tool consumes other servers.
4. Production URL, HTTPS and a Bearer token, always.
5. You don't control the client, so put safety inside the workflow: read-only first, minimal data.
6. Trust third-party servers like software you install: check who made them, and scope them narrowly.

*Lesson 4.6 complete!* _MCP: Plugging Agents Into Anything_ is done and saved to your progress, on WhatsApp and in the app.

Next up: Lesson 4.7, _Multi-Agent Systems_.
